analysis.one_liner: Raises Social Security taxes on high earners and boosts benefits for low earners and long-time beneficiaries.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in August 2021, referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, drew no cosponsors, and never received a hearing or vote before the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would gradually raise the Social Security payroll tax rate from 6.2% to 6.5% on both workers and employers, and phase out the earnings cap (about $148,200 in 2021) so that wages above it would eventually be taxed for Social Security like all other wages [S2] [S3]. The added revenue funds new benefits: a minimum benefit tied to the poverty line for people who worked many years at low wages, an extra benefit (reaching 5% after 20 years) for people who draw benefits for a long time, and continued child benefits for full-time students up to age 26 instead of cutting off around 19 [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Lifetime low earners get a new minimum benefit pegged to the poverty line, scaled up by years worked; people who receive benefits for 16 or more years get an added 5% boost; children of retired, disabled, or deceased workers who are full-time college students could keep benefits to age 26; and the benefit formula would credit earnings above the old cap, slightly raising benefits for high earners. All workers gain from a somewhat better-funded program.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Low earners, longtime beneficiaries, and student dependents

how_it_helps.text: Establishes a special minimum benefit tied to the federal poverty guideline for lifetime low earners, phased in by years in the workforce (36.7% of the poverty amount at 11 years, 100% at 30 or more), counting up to five years of child caregiving as work years [S3].
Adds a benefit increase for people who have been eligible for Social Security for at least 16 years, rising to a full 5% of their benefit at 20 or more years [S3].

Lets a child of a retired, disabled, or deceased worker keep receiving benefits through age 26 while a full-time post-secondary student, instead of benefits ending around age 19 for most students [S2] [S3].

Phases out the taxable earnings cap over ten years (90% of wages above the cap taxed in 2022, fully taxable after 2031) and raises the combined worker-employer payroll tax rate from 6.2% to 6.5% by 2027, directing the revenue to these benefit increases and the trust fund [S2] [S3].
Provides that the new benefit increases do not count as income for Medicaid, SNAP, or other means-tested programs, so low-income beneficiaries would not lose other aid because of them [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Higher earners pay the most: wages above roughly $148,200 would become subject to Social Security tax, phased in over a decade, and high earners would also see the rate increase on all their wages. Every worker and employer pays a slightly higher payroll tax rate (6.2% to 6.5%), and self-employed people would see their combined rate rise from 12.4% to 13%. Employers would likely pass part of their share to workers through lower wages over time.
analysis.who_pays_short: High earners, plus all workers and employers slightly

drawbacks.text: The payroll tax rate increase applies to every worker's wages, not just high earners, so a middle-income worker would pay about 0.3 points more out of every paycheck by 2027, and employers pay a matching increase that economists expect to be partly passed back to workers through slower wage growth [S3].

Phasing out the earnings cap applies a 6.5% tax to wages above roughly $148,200 without any corresponding increase in the maximum benefit formula proportionate to that tax (earnings above the cap earn only a 3% benefit factor), so for the highest earners the bill functions largely as a tax increase [S3].

The bill contains no mechanism to cover the transition costs if Congress later changed course, and opponents of expanding payroll taxes argue higher employment taxes can reduce hiring; this is the standard objection to any payroll-tax-financed expansion and was part of why similar proposals face resistance [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is straightforwardly redistributive within Social Security: it asks the highest earners and employers to pay somewhat more and directs the money to the poorest beneficiaries, longtime beneficiaries, and student dependents, while modestly strengthening the trust fund. The costs are real — a tax increase on high earners phased over a decade and a small rate increase for everyone — but the design is conventional and the low-income provisions are targeted without complicated phase-outs that would punish work. The main honest criticism is that it raises taxes on middle-income workers too, not only the wealthy, and that any payroll tax increase has some effect on hiring and wages.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and its Social Security subcommittee in August 2021 and sat there with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote through the end of the Congress in January 2023 [S1] [S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Gwen Moore introduced the Social Security Enhancement and Protection Act on August 17, 2021 [S1] [S5].
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means and to its Subcommittee on Social Security [S5].
No further action was taken; the bill died in committee when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never advanced, the tax rules it would have changed stayed in place: wages above roughly $148,200 remained exempt from Social Security tax, and the payroll rate stayed at 6.2%. High earners and employers who would have paid more are better off; low earners, longtime beneficiaries, and student dependents get nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High earners above the payroll tax cap

for.name: Rep. Gwen Moore
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its only sponsor; it was referred to Ways and Means the same day.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. Richard Neal (D-MA)
against.what_they_did: Held the bill for the remainder of the 117th Congress without a hearing, markup, or vote.

against.name: House leadership
against.role: Speaker and majority leadership of the 117th House
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the House floor or prioritized it for committee action before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and the bill drew zero cosponsors, so its partisan support never took shape in the record [S4].

industries.industry: High earners (households with wages above the Social Security tax cap)
industries.note: Wages above roughly $148,200 would become subject to Social Security tax over ten years, on top of a slightly higher rate. Their benefit formula would also gain a 3% factor on earnings above the cap, but far less than proportionate to the tax.
Employers pay a matching payroll tax, which would rise from 6.2% to 6.5% and extend above the earnings cap. Part of this cost typically shifts to workers through lower wages over time.

industries.industry: Self-employed workers and small business owners
industries.note: Self-employment tax would rise from 12.4% to 13% and apply to earnings above the cap once it is phased out, hitting freelancers and small business owners with above-cap income hardest.
